overview: Dreadnoughtus schrani is a massive titanosaur sauropod from the Late Cretaceous Cerro Fortaleza Formation of Patagonia, Argentina (~77 Ma). The holotype specimen — described in 2014 by Kenneth Lacovara and colleagues — is the most complete giant titanosaur known, with 70% of the skeleton by skeletal element count. Mass estimates range from 38 to 65 tonnes, making it one of the heaviest terrestrial animals documented.

The name "dread nothing" reflects the assessment that a fully grown individual would have had no natural predators. The holotype preserves bone textures indicating the animal was still growing at death, suggesting adult Dreadnoughtus could have been even heavier. It represents the culmination of the titanosaur trend toward gigantism that characterised Late Cretaceous South America.

fossilSites.name: Cerro Fortaleza Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Cretaceous (Campanian) fluvial deposits preserving the most complete giant titanosaur skeleton known.

articles.title: Discovery and description
articles.body: Kenneth Lacovara's team excavated Dreadnoughtus schrani between 2005 and 2009 from Patagonia. Two individuals were found; the larger (holotype) preserves 70% of skeletal elements by count — exceptional for a giant titanosaur. The 2014 description included a detailed biomechanical and phylogenetic analysis. Bone surface texture (rapid growth surfaces) confirmed the individual was sub-adult at death.

articles.title: Mass and size
articles.body: Mass estimates from limb bone scaling place Dreadnoughtus between 38 and 65 tonnes, depending on the scaling equation used. Body length is estimated at 26 metres. These figures place it among the heaviest land animals ever, though Patagotitan mayorum (described 2017, ~69 tonnes) and the fragmentary Argentinosaurus may have been heavier. The uncertainty in all such estimates reflects the difficulty of recovering truly complete giant titanosaur material.

articles.title: Titanosaur gigantism
articles.body: Titanosaurs repeatedly evolved enormous body sizes in the Cretaceous, particularly in South America. The ecological drivers of this trend are debated: abundant vegetation, evasion of predators through size (abelisaurids rarely attacked very large titanosaurs), or resource availability during a period of high global productivity. Titanosaurs also showed unusually rapid postnatal growth — reaching adult size within a few decades from egg-sized hatchlings.

fossilRecord.material: Two partial skeletons, including a very large individual with extensive postcranial material.
fossilRecord.evidence: Limb, vertebral and girdle bones provide unusually strong mass estimates for a giant titanosaur.

consensusScope: diet, locomotion and major uncertainty wording

record.mya: Campanian-Maastrichtian, broadly about 84-66 million years ago
record.description: Dreadnoughtus schrani was a giant titanosaur from the Cerro Fortaleza Formation of Patagonia. Two individuals are known, including one associated partial skeleton preserving much of the limbs, girdles and tail but no complete skull, neck or articulated trunk.
facts: The principal specimen is substantial but not the exceptionally high percentage once claimed when counted by every repeated tail bone.
The original mass estimate near 59 tonnes was challenged by volumetric and scaling studies; no single mass value is consensus.
Bone histology indicates the main individual was still growing.

review.ageReviewNote: The Cerro Fortaleza Formation is Late Cretaceous, but its numerical age is poorly constrained across a wide Campanian-Maastrichtian interval.

residualUncertainty: Formation age, body mass and exact titanosaur relationships remain debated.
The skull and much of the neck and torso are unknown.

evidence.material: Two partial skeletons, one substantial associated postcranium dominated by limbs, girdles and caudals.
evidence.confidenceLimit: High for preserved anatomy and giant size; moderate for growth; low-to-moderate for exact mass, age and skull.
